name: Deploy Production

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

permissions:
  contents: read
  packages: write

concurrency:
  group: deploy-production
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    timeout-minutes: 30

    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0

      - name: Load versioned Hetzner deploy config
        run: |
          ruby <<'RUBY' >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
          require File.expand_path("app/lib/hetzner_deploy_config.rb", Dir.pwd)

          puts "APP_HOST=#{HetznerDeployConfig.app_host}"
          puts "KAMAL_WEB_HOST=#{HetznerDeployConfig.web_host}"
          puts "KAMAL_SSH_HOST_KEY=#{HetznerDeployConfig.ssh_host_key}"
          RUBY

      - name: Set up Ruby
        uses: ruby/setup-ruby@v1
        with:
          ruby-version: .ruby-version
          bundler-cache: true

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v4

      - name: Log in to GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@v4
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ github.token }}

      - name: Build and push app image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          platforms: linux/amd64
          tags: |
            ghcr.io/marcbey/stuttgart-live-de:${{ github.sha }}
            ghcr.io/marcbey/stuttgart-live-de:latest
          labels: |
            service=stuttgart_live_de
            org.opencontainers.image.source=https://github.com/marcbey/stuttgart-live.de

      - name: Prepare Kamal secrets for GitHub Actions
        env:
          MEDIA_PROXY_SECRET: ${{ secrets.MEDIA_PROXY_SECRET }}
        run: |
          cat > .kamal/secrets.hetzner <<'EOF'
          KAMAL_REGISTRY_PUSH_TOKEN=$KAMAL_REGISTRY_PUSH_TOKEN
          KAMAL_REGISTRY_PULL_PASSWORD=$KAMAL_REGISTRY_PULL_PASSWORD
          RAILS_MASTER_KEY=$RAILS_MASTER_KEY
          DB_PASSWORD=REDACTED
          MEDIA_PROXY_SECRET=$MEDIA_PROXY_SECRET
          EOF

      - name: Prepare SSH access
        env:
          KAMAL_SSH_PRIVATE_KEY: ${{ secrets.KAMAL_SSH_PRIVATE_KEY }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail

          install -d -m 700 ~/.ssh
          printf '%s\n' "$KAMAL_SSH_PRIVATE_KEY" > "$RUNNER_TEMP/kamal.key"
          chmod 600 "$RUNNER_TEMP/kamal.key"

          host="${KAMAL_WEB_HOST}"
          if [ -z "${KAMAL_SSH_HOST_KEY}" ]; then
            echo "KAMAL_SSH_HOST_KEY fehlt" >&2
            exit 1
          fi
          ssh-keygen -R "$host" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
          printf '%s\n' "$KAMAL_SSH_HOST_KEY" >> ~/.ssh/known_hosts

      - name: Ensure compatible kamal-proxy version
        env:
          KAMAL_SSH_KEY_PATH: ${{ runner.temp }}/kamal.key
          KAMAL_REGISTRY_PUSH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          KAMAL_REGISTRY_PULL_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.KAMAL_REGISTRY_PULL_PASSWORD }}
          RAILS_MASTER_KEY: ${{ secrets.RAILS_MASTER_KEY }}
          DB_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.DB_PASSWORD }}
          MEDIA_PROXY_SECRET: ${{ secrets.MEDIA_PROXY_SECRET }}
          REQUIRED_KAMAL_PROXY_VERSION: v0.9.2
          KAMAL_SKIP_REMOTE_REGISTRY_LOGIN: true
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail

          host="${KAMAL_WEB_HOST}"
          current_proxy_image="$(
            ssh -i "$KAMAL_SSH_KEY_PATH" -o StrictHostKeyChecking=yes deploy@"$host" \
              "docker inspect kamal-proxy --format '{{.Config.Image}}' 2>/dev/null || true"
          )"
          current_proxy_version="${current_proxy_image##*:}"

          if [ -z "$current_proxy_image" ]; then
            echo "kamal-proxy läuft noch nicht, starte ihn mit bin/kamal proxy reboot"
            bin/kamal proxy reboot -d hetzner
            exit 0
          fi

          if [ "$current_proxy_version" = "$REQUIRED_KAMAL_PROXY_VERSION" ]; then
            echo "kamal-proxy ist bereits auf $current_proxy_version"
            exit 0
          fi

          lowest_version="$(
            printf '%s\n%s\n' "$REQUIRED_KAMAL_PROXY_VERSION" "$current_proxy_version" | sort -V | head -n1
          )"
          if [ "$lowest_version" = "$REQUIRED_KAMAL_PROXY_VERSION" ]; then
            echo "kamal-proxy ist bereits kompatibel ($current_proxy_version)"
            exit 0
          fi

          echo "kamal-proxy ist zu alt ($current_proxy_version), aktualisiere auf mindestens $REQUIRED_KAMAL_PROXY_VERSION"
          bin/kamal proxy reboot -d hetzner

      - name: Deploy with Kamal
        env:
          KAMAL_SSH_KEY_PATH: ${{ runner.temp }}/kamal.key
          KAMAL_REGISTRY_PUSH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          KAMAL_REGISTRY_PULL_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.KAMAL_REGISTRY_PULL_PASSWORD }}
          RAILS_MASTER_KEY: ${{ secrets.RAILS_MASTER_KEY }}
          DB_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.DB_PASSWORD }}
          MEDIA_PROXY_SECRET: ${{ secrets.MEDIA_PROXY_SECRET }}
          SENTRY_RELEASE: ${{ github.sha }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail

          # GitHub-Secrets dürfen hier keine Zeilenumbrüche enthalten.
          export KAMAL_REGISTRY_PUSH_TOKEN="$(printf '%s' "$KAMAL_REGISTRY_PUSH_TOKEN" | tr -d '\r\n')"
          export KAMAL_REGISTRY_PULL_PASSWORD="$(printf '%s' "$KAMAL_REGISTRY_PULL_PASSWORD" | tr -d '\r\n')"
          export MEDIA_PROXY_SECRET="$(printf '%s' "$MEDIA_PROXY_SECRET" | tr -d '\r\n')"
          export KAMAL_SKIP_REMOTE_REGISTRY_LOGIN=true

          host="${KAMAL_WEB_HOST}"
          # Der Remote-Host braucht weiterhin ein stabiles GHCR-Credential für Pulls.
          printf '%s' "$KAMAL_REGISTRY_PULL_PASSWORD" | \
            ssh -i "$KAMAL_SSH_KEY_PATH" -o StrictHostKeyChecking=yes deploy@"$host" \
              "docker login ghcr.io -u marcbey --password-stdin"

          deploy_log="$RUNNER_TEMP/kamal-deploy.log"
          max_attempts=3

          run_deploy() {
            bin/kamal deploy -d hetzner --skip_push 2>&1 | tee "$deploy_log"
          }

          transient_registry_failure() {
            grep -Eq \
              'TLS handshake timeout|Client\\.Timeout exceeded|i/o timeout|unexpected EOF|connection reset by peer|dial tcp.*:443: connect: connection timed out' \
              "$deploy_log"
          }

          attempt=1
          while true; do
            if run_deploy; then
              exit 0
            fi

            if [ "$attempt" -ge "$max_attempts" ] || ! transient_registry_failure; then
              break
            fi

            echo "Temporärer GHCR-Pull-Fehler erkannt, warte 15 Sekunden und versuche Deploy erneut ($attempt/$max_attempts)"
            sleep 15
            attempt=$((attempt + 1))
          done

          if ! grep -Fq "kamal-proxy version" "$deploy_log"; then
            exit 1
          fi

          echo "kamal-proxy ist veraltet, führe Proxy-Reboot aus und wiederhole Deploy"
          bin/kamal proxy reboot -d hetzner
          bin/kamal deploy -d hetzner --skip_push

      - name: Notify Sentry about deployed release
        env:
          SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN }}
          SENTRY_ORG: ${{ vars.SENTRY_ORG }}
          SENTRY_PROJECT: ${{ vars.SENTRY_PROJECT }}
          SENTRY_RELEASE: ${{ github.sha }}
          SENTRY_ENVIRONMENT: production
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail

          if [ -z "${SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN}" ]; then
require "yaml"

module HetznerDeployConfig
  CONFIG_PATH = File.expand_path("../../config/deploy.hetzner.shared.yml", __dir__)
  MissingConfigError = Class.new(StandardError)

  class << self
    def app_host
      fetch("app_host")
    end

    def app_host_if_present
      fetch("app_host", required: false)
    end

    def web_host
      fetch("web_host")
    end

    def ssh_host_key
      fetch("ssh_host_key")
    end

    def fetch(key, required: true)
      loaded_config = config(required:)
      return unless loaded_config

      loaded_config.fetch(key)
    end

    private

    def config(required: true)
      return @config if instance_variable_defined?(:@config)

      unless File.exist?(config_path)
        if required
          raise MissingConfigError, "Missing Hetzner deploy config at #{config_path}"
        end

        @config = nil
        return
      end

      @config = YAML.safe_load_file(config_path) || {}
    end

    def config_path
      CONFIG_PATH
    end
  end
end

set -euo pipefail

APP_ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)"
cd "$APP_ROOT"

if [[ -f .env ]]; then
  set -a
  # shellcheck disable=SC1091
  source .env
  set +a
fi

fail() {
  printf 'Fehler: %s\n' "$1" >&2
  exit 1
}

require_file() {
  local path="$1"
  [[ -f "$path" ]] || fail "Datei fehlt: $path"
}

require_value() {
  local name="$1"
  [[ -n "${!name:-}" ]] || fail "Umgebungsvariable fehlt oder ist leer: $name"
}

read_deploy_config_value() {
  local key="$1"

  ruby - "$key" <<'RUBY'
require File.expand_path("app/lib/hetzner_deploy_config.rb", Dir.pwd)

puts HetznerDeployConfig.fetch(ARGV.fetch(0))
RUBY
}

extract_secret_names() {
  ruby <<'RUBY'
require "yaml"
require "erb"

config_path = File.expand_path("config/deploy.hetzner.yml", Dir.pwd)
raw = ERB.new(File.read(config_path)).result
config = YAML.safe_load(raw, aliases: true)
Array(config.dig("registry", "password")).each { |name| puts name }
Array(config.dig("env", "secret")).each { |name| puts name }
RUBY
}

printf 'Prüfe lokale Hetzner-Voraussetzungen in %s\n' "$APP_ROOT"

require_file "config/master.key"
require_file "config/deploy.hetzner.shared.yml"
require_file ".kamal/secrets.hetzner"
require_file "$HOME/.ssh/stgt-live-hetzner-github"

app_host="$(read_deploy_config_value "app_host")"
web_host="$(read_deploy_config_value "web_host")"

while IFS= read -r secret_name; do
  [[ -n "$secret_name" ]] || continue
  if ! grep -Eq "^${secret_name}=" ".kamal/secrets.hetzner"; then
    fail "Secret fehlt in .kamal/secrets.hetzner: ${secret_name}"
  fi
done < <(extract_secret_names)

printf 'APP_HOST: %s\n' "$app_host"
printf 'KAMAL_WEB_HOST: %s\n' "$web_host"
printf 'Kamal-Secrets: vollständig\n'
printf 'SSH-Key: %s\n' "$HOME/.ssh/stgt-live-hetzner-github"
printf 'Status: OK\n'

name: Deploy Production

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

permissions:
  contents: read
  packages: write

concurrency:
  group: deploy-production
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    timeout-minutes: 30

    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0

      - name: Load versioned Hetzner deploy config
        run: |
          ruby <<'RUBY' >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
          require File.expand_path("app/lib/hetzner_deploy_config.rb", Dir.pwd)

          puts "APP_HOST=#{HetznerDeployConfig.app_host}"
          puts "KAMAL_WEB_HOST=#{HetznerDeployConfig.web_host}"
          puts "KAMAL_SSH_HOST_KEY=#{HetznerDeployConfig.ssh_host_key}"
          RUBY

      - name: Set up Ruby
        uses: ruby/setup-ruby@v1
        with:
          ruby-version: .ruby-version
          bundler-cache: true

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v4

      - name: Log in to GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@v4
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: ${{ github.actor }}
          password: ${{ github.token }}

      - name: Build and push app image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          platforms: linux/amd64
          tags: |
            ghcr.io/marcbey/stuttgart-live-de:${{ github.sha }}
            ghcr.io/marcbey/stuttgart-live-de:latest
          labels: |
            service=stuttgart_live_de
            org.opencontainers.image.source=https://github.com/marcbey/stuttgart-live.de

      - name: Prepare Kamal secrets for GitHub Actions
        env:
          MEDIA_PROXY_SECRET: ${{ secrets.MEDIA_PROXY_SECRET }}
        run: |
          cat > .kamal/secrets.hetzner <<'EOF'
          KAMAL_REGISTRY_PUSH_TOKEN=$KAMAL_REGISTRY_PUSH_TOKEN
          KAMAL_REGISTRY_PULL_PASSWORD=$KAMAL_REGISTRY_PULL_PASSWORD
          RAILS_MASTER_KEY=$RAILS_MASTER_KEY
          DB_PASSWORD=REDACTED
          MEDIA_PROXY_SECRET=$MEDIA_PROXY_SECRET
          EOF

      - name: Prepare SSH access
        env:
          KAMAL_SSH_PRIVATE_KEY: ${{ secrets.KAMAL_SSH_PRIVATE_KEY }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail

          install -d -m 700 ~/.ssh
          printf '%s\n' "$KAMAL_SSH_PRIVATE_KEY" > "$RUNNER_TEMP/kamal.key"
          chmod 600 "$RUNNER_TEMP/kamal.key"

          host="${KAMAL_WEB_HOST}"
          if [ -z "${KAMAL_SSH_HOST_KEY}" ]; then
            echo "KAMAL_SSH_HOST_KEY fehlt" >&2
            exit 1
          fi
          ssh-keygen -R "$host" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
          printf '%s\n' "$KAMAL_SSH_HOST_KEY" >> ~/.ssh/known_hosts

      - name: Ensure compatible kamal-proxy version
        env:
          KAMAL_SSH_KEY_PATH: ${{ runner.temp }}/kamal.key
          KAMAL_REGISTRY_PUSH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          KAMAL_REGISTRY_PULL_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.KAMAL_REGISTRY_PULL_PASSWORD }}
          RAILS_MASTER_KEY: ${{ secrets.RAILS_MASTER_KEY }}
          DB_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.DB_PASSWORD }}
          MEDIA_PROXY_SECRET: ${{ secrets.MEDIA_PROXY_SECRET }}
          REQUIRED_KAMAL_PROXY_VERSION: v0.9.2
          KAMAL_SKIP_REMOTE_REGISTRY_LOGIN: true
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail

          host="${KAMAL_WEB_HOST}"
          current_proxy_image="$(
            ssh -i "$KAMAL_SSH_KEY_PATH" -o StrictHostKeyChecking=yes deploy@"$host" \
              "docker inspect kamal-proxy --format '{{.Config.Image}}' 2>/dev/null || true"
          )"
          current_proxy_version="${current_proxy_image##*:}"

          if [ -z "$current_proxy_image" ]; then
            echo "kamal-proxy läuft noch nicht, starte ihn mit bin/kamal proxy reboot"
            bin/kamal proxy reboot -d hetzner
            exit 0
          fi

          if [ "$current_proxy_version" = "$REQUIRED_KAMAL_PROXY_VERSION" ]; then
            echo "kamal-proxy ist bereits auf $current_proxy_version"
            exit 0
          fi

          lowest_version="$(
            printf '%s\n%s\n' "$REQUIRED_KAMAL_PROXY_VERSION" "$current_proxy_version" | sort -V | head -n1
          )"
          if [ "$lowest_version" = "$REQUIRED_KAMAL_PROXY_VERSION" ]; then
            echo "kamal-proxy ist bereits kompatibel ($current_proxy_version)"
            exit 0
          fi

          echo "kamal-proxy ist zu alt ($current_proxy_version), aktualisiere auf mindestens $REQUIRED_KAMAL_PROXY_VERSION"
          bin/kamal proxy reboot -d hetzner

      - name: Deploy with Kamal
        env:
          KAMAL_SSH_KEY_PATH: ${{ runner.temp }}/kamal.key
          KAMAL_REGISTRY_PUSH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
          KAMAL_REGISTRY_PULL_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.KAMAL_REGISTRY_PULL_PASSWORD }}
          RAILS_MASTER_KEY: ${{ secrets.RAILS_MASTER_KEY }}
          DB_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.DB_PASSWORD }}
          MEDIA_PROXY_SECRET: ${{ secrets.MEDIA_PROXY_SECRET }}
          SENTRY_RELEASE: ${{ github.sha }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail

          # GitHub-Secrets dürfen hier keine Zeilenumbrüche enthalten.
          export KAMAL_REGISTRY_PUSH_TOKEN="$(printf '%s' "$KAMAL_REGISTRY_PUSH_TOKEN" | tr -d '\r\n')"
          export KAMAL_REGISTRY_PULL_PASSWORD="$(printf '%s' "$KAMAL_REGISTRY_PULL_PASSWORD" | tr -d '\r\n')"
          export MEDIA_PROXY_SECRET="$(printf '%s' "$MEDIA_PROXY_SECRET" | tr -d '\r\n')"
          export KAMAL_SKIP_REMOTE_REGISTRY_LOGIN=true

          host="${KAMAL_WEB_HOST}"
          # Der Remote-Host braucht weiterhin ein stabiles GHCR-Credential für Pulls.
          printf '%s' "$KAMAL_REGISTRY_PULL_PASSWORD" | \
            ssh -i "$KAMAL_SSH_KEY_PATH" -o StrictHostKeyChecking=yes deploy@"$host" \
              "docker login ghcr.io -u marcbey --password-stdin"

          deploy_log="$RUNNER_TEMP/kamal-deploy.log"
          max_attempts=3

          run_deploy() {
            bin/kamal deploy -d hetzner --skip_push 2>&1 | tee "$deploy_log"
          }

          transient_registry_failure() {
            grep -Eq \
              'TLS handshake timeout|Client\\.Timeout exceeded|i/o timeout|unexpected EOF|connection reset by peer|dial tcp.*:443: connect: connection timed out' \
              "$deploy_log"
          }

          attempt=1
          while true; do
            if run_deploy; then
              exit 0
            fi

            if [ "$attempt" -ge "$max_attempts" ] || ! transient_registry_failure; then
              break
            fi

            echo "Temporärer GHCR-Pull-Fehler erkannt, warte 15 Sekunden und versuche Deploy erneut ($attempt/$max_attempts)"
            sleep 15
            attempt=$((attempt + 1))
          done

          if ! grep -Fq "kamal-proxy version" "$deploy_log"; then
            exit 1
          fi

          echo "kamal-proxy ist veraltet, führe Proxy-Reboot aus und wiederhole Deploy"
          bin/kamal proxy reboot -d hetzner
          bin/kamal deploy -d hetzner --skip_push

      - name: Notify Sentry about deployed release
        env:
          SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN }}
          SENTRY_ORG: ${{ vars.SENTRY_ORG }}
          SENTRY_PROJECT: ${{ vars.SENTRY_PROJECT }}
          SENTRY_RELEASE: ${{ github.sha }}
          SENTRY_ENVIRONMENT: production
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail

          if [ -z "${SENTRY_AUTH_TOKEN}" ]; then
require "yaml"

module HetznerDeployConfig
  CONFIG_PATH = File.expand_path("../../config/deploy.hetzner.shared.yml", __dir__)
  MissingConfigError = Class.new(StandardError)

  class << self
    def app_host
      fetch("app_host")
    end

    def app_host_if_present
      fetch("app_host", required: false)
    end

    def web_host
      fetch("web_host")
    end

    def ssh_host_key
      fetch("ssh_host_key")
    end

    def fetch(key, required: true)
      loaded_config = config(required:)
      return unless loaded_config

      loaded_config.fetch(key)
    end

    private

    def config(required: true)
      return @config if instance_variable_defined?(:@config)

      unless File.exist?(config_path)
        if required
          raise MissingConfigError, "Missing Hetzner deploy config at #{config_path}"
        end

        @config = nil
        return
      end

      @config = YAML.safe_load_file(config_path) || {}
    end

    def config_path
      CONFIG_PATH
    end
  end
end
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail

APP_ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.." && pwd)"
cd "$APP_ROOT"

if [[ -f .env ]]; then
  set -a
  # shellcheck disable=SC1091
  source .env
  set +a
fi

fail() {
  printf 'Fehler: %s\n' "$1" >&2
  exit 1
}

require_file() {
  local path="$1"
  [[ -f "$path" ]] || fail "Datei fehlt: $path"
}

require_value() {
  local name="$1"
  [[ -n "${!name:-}" ]] || fail "Umgebungsvariable fehlt oder ist leer: $name"
}

read_deploy_config_value() {
  local key="$1"

  ruby - "$key" <<'RUBY'
require File.expand_path("app/lib/hetzner_deploy_config.rb", Dir.pwd)

puts HetznerDeployConfig.fetch(ARGV.fetch(0))
RUBY
}

extract_secret_names() {
  ruby <<'RUBY'
require "yaml"
require "erb"

config_path = File.expand_path("config/deploy.hetzner.yml", Dir.pwd)
raw = ERB.new(File.read(config_path)).result
config = YAML.safe_load(raw, aliases: true)
Array(config.dig("registry", "password")).each { |name| puts name }
Array(config.dig("env", "secret")).each { |name| puts name }
RUBY
}

printf 'Prüfe lokale Hetzner-Voraussetzungen in %s\n' "$APP_ROOT"

require_file "config/master.key"
require_file "config/deploy.hetzner.shared.yml"
require_file ".kamal/secrets.hetzner"
require_file "$HOME/.ssh/stgt-live-hetzner-github"

app_host="$(read_deploy_config_value "app_host")"
web_host="$(read_deploy_config_value "web_host")"

while IFS= read -r secret_name; do
  [[ -n "$secret_name" ]] || continue
  if ! grep -Eq "^${secret_name}=" ".kamal/secrets.hetzner"; then
    fail "Secret fehlt in .kamal/secrets.hetzner: ${secret_name}"
  fi
done < <(extract_secret_names)

printf 'APP_HOST: %s\n' "$app_host"
printf 'KAMAL_WEB_HOST: %s\n' "$web_host"
printf 'Kamal-Secrets: vollständig\n'
printf 'SSH-Key: %s\n' "$HOME/.ssh/stgt-live-hetzner-github"
printf 'Status: OK\n'

name: Deploy Production

on:
  workflow_dispatch:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

permissions:
  contents: read
  packages: write

concurrency:
  group: deploy-production
  cancel-in-progress: false

jobs:
  deploy:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment: production
    timeout-minutes: 30

    steps:
      - name: Checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v7
        with:
          fetch-depth: 0

      - name: Load versioned Hetzner deploy config
        run: |
          ruby <<'RUBY' >> "$GITHUB_ENV"
          require File.expand_path("app/lib/hetzner_deploy_config.rb", Dir.pwd)

          puts "APP_HOST=#{HetznerDeployConfig.app_host}"
          puts "KAMAL_WEB_HOST=#{HetznerDeployConfig.web_host}"
          puts "KAMAL_SSH_HOST_KEY=#{HetznerDeployConfig.ssh_host_key}"
          RUBY

      - name: Set up Ruby
        uses: ruby/setup-ruby@v1
        with:
          ruby-version: .ruby-version
          bundler-cache: true

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v4

      - name: Log in to GHCR
        uses: docker/login-action@v4
        with:
          registry: ghcr.io
          username: marcbey
          password: ${{ secrets.KAMAL_REGISTRY_PUSH_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build and push app image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v7
        with:
          context: .
          push: true
          platforms: linux/amd64
          tags: |
            ghcr.io/marcbey/russ-live-de:${{ github.sha }}
            ghcr.io/marcbey/russ-live-de:latest
          labels: |
            service=russ_live_de
            org.opencontainers.image.source=https://github.com/marcbey/russ-live.de

      - name: Prepare Kamal secrets for GitHub Actions
        run: |
          cat > .kamal/secrets.hetzner <<'EOF'
          KAMAL_REGISTRY_PUSH_TOKEN=$KAMAL_REGISTRY_PUSH_TOKEN
          KAMAL_REGISTRY_PULL_PASSWORD=$KAMAL_REGISTRY_PULL_PASSWORD
          RAILS_MASTER_KEY=$RAILS_MASTER_KEY
          RUSS_LIVE_PRIMARY_DB_PASSWORD=REDACTED          RUSS_LIVE_OPERATIONAL_DB_PASSWORD=REDACTED          MEDIA_PROXY_SECRET=$MEDIA_PROXY_SECRET
          EOF

      - name: Prepare SSH access
        env:
          KAMAL_SSH_PRIVATE_KEY: ${{ secrets.KAMAL_SSH_PRIVATE_KEY }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail

          install -d -m 700 ~/.ssh
          printf '%s\n' "$KAMAL_SSH_PRIVATE_KEY" > "$RUNNER_TEMP/kamal.key"
          chmod 600 "$RUNNER_TEMP/kamal.key"

          host="${KAMAL_WEB_HOST}"
          if [ -z "${KAMAL_SSH_HOST_KEY}" ]; then
            echo "KAMAL_SSH_HOST_KEY fehlt" >&2
            exit 1
          fi
          ssh-keygen -R "$host" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true
          printf '%s\n' "$KAMAL_SSH_HOST_KEY" >> ~/.ssh/known_hosts

      - name: Ensure compatible kamal-proxy version
        env:
          KAMAL_SSH_KEY_PATH: ${{ runner.temp }}/kamal.key
          KAMAL_REGISTRY_PUSH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.KAMAL_REGISTRY_PUSH_TOKEN }}
          KAMAL_REGISTRY_PULL_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.KAMAL_REGISTRY_PULL_PASSWORD }}
          RAILS_MASTER_KEY: ${{ secrets.RAILS_MASTER_KEY }}
          RUSS_LIVE_PRIMARY_DB_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.RUSS_LIVE_PRIMARY_DB_PASSWORD }}
          RUSS_LIVE_OPERATIONAL_DB_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.RUSS_LIVE_OPERATIONAL_DB_PASSWORD }}
          MEDIA_PROXY_SECRET: ${{ secrets.MEDIA_PROXY_SECRET }}
          REQUIRED_KAMAL_PROXY_VERSION: v0.9.2
          KAMAL_SKIP_REMOTE_REGISTRY_LOGIN: true
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail

          host="${KAMAL_WEB_HOST}"
          current_proxy_image="$(
            ssh -i "$KAMAL_SSH_KEY_PATH" -o StrictHostKeyChecking=yes deploy@"$host" \
              "docker inspect kamal-proxy --format '{{.Config.Image}}' 2>/dev/null || true"
          )"
          current_proxy_version="${current_proxy_image##*:}"

          if [ -z "$current_proxy_image" ]; then
            echo "kamal-proxy läuft noch nicht, starte ihn mit bin/kamal proxy reboot"
            bin/kamal proxy reboot -d hetzner
            exit 0
          fi

          if [ "$current_proxy_version" = "$REQUIRED_KAMAL_PROXY_VERSION" ]; then
            echo "kamal-proxy ist bereits auf $current_proxy_version"
            exit 0
          fi

          lowest_version="$(
            printf '%s\n%s\n' "$REQUIRED_KAMAL_PROXY_VERSION" "$current_proxy_version" | sort -V | head -n1
          )"
          if [ "$lowest_version" = "$REQUIRED_KAMAL_PROXY_VERSION" ]; then
            echo "kamal-proxy ist bereits kompatibel ($current_proxy_version)"
            exit 0
          fi

          echo "kamal-proxy ist zu alt ($current_proxy_version), aktualisiere auf mindestens $REQUIRED_KAMAL_PROXY_VERSION"
          bin/kamal proxy reboot -d hetzner

      - name: Deploy with Kamal
        env:
          KAMAL_SSH_KEY_PATH: ${{ runner.temp }}/kamal.key
          KAMAL_REGISTRY_PUSH_TOKEN: ${{ secrets.KAMAL_REGISTRY_PUSH_TOKEN }}
          KAMAL_REGISTRY_PULL_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.KAMAL_REGISTRY_PULL_PASSWORD }}
          RAILS_MASTER_KEY: ${{ secrets.RAILS_MASTER_KEY }}
          RUSS_LIVE_PRIMARY_DB_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.RUSS_LIVE_PRIMARY_DB_PASSWORD }}
          RUSS_LIVE_OPERATIONAL_DB_PASSWORD: ${{ secrets.RUSS_LIVE_OPERATIONAL_DB_PASSWORD }}
          MEDIA_PROXY_SECRET: ${{ secrets.MEDIA_PROXY_SECRET }}
        run: |
          set -euo pipefail

          # GitHub-Secrets dürfen hier keine Zeilenumbrüche enthalten.
          export KAMAL_REGISTRY_PUSH_TOKEN="$(printf '%s' "$KAMAL_REGISTRY_PUSH_TOKEN" | tr -d '\r\n')"
          export KAMAL_REGISTRY_PULL_PASSWORD="$(printf '%s' "$KAMAL_REGISTRY_PULL_PASSWORD" | tr -d '\r\n')"
          export RUSS_LIVE_PRIMARY_DB_PASSWORD=REDACTED '%s' "$RUSS_LIVE_PRIMARY_DB_PASSWORD" | tr -d '\r\n')"
          export RUSS_LIVE_OPERATIONAL_DB_PASSWORD=REDACTED '%s' "$RUSS_LIVE_OPERATIONAL_DB_PASSWORD" | tr -d '\r\n')"
          export MEDIA_PROXY_SECRET="$(printf '%s' "$MEDIA_PROXY_SECRET" | tr -d '\r\n')"
          export KAMAL_SKIP_REMOTE_REGISTRY_LOGIN=true

          host="${KAMAL_WEB_HOST}"
          # Der Remote-Host braucht weiterhin ein stabiles GHCR-Credential für Pulls.
          printf '%s' "$KAMAL_REGISTRY_PULL_PASSWORD" | \
            ssh -i "$KAMAL_SSH_KEY_PATH" -o StrictHostKeyChecking=yes deploy@"$host" \
              "docker login ghcr.io -u marcbey --password-stdin"

          deploy_log="$RUNNER_TEMP/kamal-deploy.log"
          max_attempts=3

          run_deploy() {
            bin/kamal deploy -d hetzner --skip_push --version "$GITHUB_SHA" 2>&1 | tee "$deploy_log"
          }

          transient_registry_failure() {
            grep -Eq \
              'TLS handshake timeout|Client\.Timeout exceeded|i/o timeout|unexpected EOF|connection reset by peer|dial tcp.*:443: connect: connection timed out' \
              "$deploy_log"
          }

          attempt=1
          while true; do

L13: If our validation checks get the right responses from your web server, the validation is considered successful and you can go on to issue your certificate. If the validation checks fail, you’ll have to try again with a new certificate.
L14: Our implementation of the HTTP-01 challenge follows redirects, up to 10 redirects deep. It only accepts redirects to “http:” or “https:”, and only to ports 80 or 443. When redirected to an HTTPS URL, it does not validate certificates (since this challenge is intended to bootstrap valid certificates, it may encounter self-signed or expired certificates along the way).
L15: The HTTP-01 challenge can only be done on port 80. Allowing clients to specify arbitrary ports would make the challenge less secure, and so it is not allowed by the ACME standard.
L16: 
L17: Pros:
L18: 
L19:   * It’s easy to automate without extra knowledge about a domain’s configuration.
L20:   * It allows hosting providers to issue certificates for domains CNAMEd to them.
L21:   * It works with off-the-shelf web servers.
L22:   * It can be used to validate IP Addresses as well.
L23: 
L24: Cons:
L25:   * It doesn’t work if your ISP blocks port 80 (this is rare, but some residential ISPs do this).
L26:   * This challenge cannot be used to issue wildcard certificates.
L27:   * If you have multiple web servers, you have to make sure the file is available on all of them.
L28: # DNS-01 challenge
L29: This challenge asks you to prove that you control the DNS for your domain name by putting a specific value in a TXT record under that domain name. It is harder to configure than HTTP-01, but can work in scenarios that HTTP-01 can’t. It also allows you to issue wildcard certificates. After Let’s Encrypt gives your ACME client a token, your client will create a TXT record derived from that token and your account key, and put that record at `_acme-challenge.<YOUR_DOMAIN>`.
L30: Then Let’s Encrypt will query the DNS system for that record. If it finds a match, you can proceed to issue a certificate!
L31: Since automation of issuance and renewals is really important, it only makes sense to use DNS-01 challenges if your DNS provider has an API you can use to automate updates. Our community has started a cite31†list of such DNS providers here†community.letsencrypt.org . Your DNS provider may be the same as your registrar (the company you bought your domain name from), or it might be different. If you want to change your DNS provider, you just need to make some small changes at your registrar.
L32: You don’t need to wait for your domain to be close to expiration to do so.
L33: Note that putting your full DNS API credentials on your web server significantly increases the impact if that web server is hacked. Best practice is to use cite32†more narrowly scoped API credentials†www.eff.org , or perform DNS validation from a separate server and automatically copy certificates to your web server.
L34: Since Let’s Encrypt follows the DNS standards when looking up TXT records for DNS-01 validation, you can use CNAME records or NS records to delegate answering the challenge to other DNS zones. This can be used to cite32†delegate the `_acme-challenge` subdomain†www.eff.org to a validation-specific server or zone. It can also be used if your DNS provider is slow to update, and you want to delegate to a quicker-updating server.
L35: Most DNS providers have a “propagation time” that governs how long it takes from the time you update a DNS record until it’s available on all of their servers. It can be hard to measure this because they often also use cite33†anycast†en.wikipedia.org , which means multiple servers can have the same IP address, and depending on where you are in the world you might talk to a different server (and get a different answer) than Let’s Encrypt does.
L36: The best DNS APIs provide a way for you to automatically check whether an update is fully propagated. If your DNS provider doesn’t have this, you just have to configure your client to wait long enough (often as much as an hour) to ensure the update is propagated before triggering validation.
L37: You can have multiple TXT records in place for the same name. For instance, this might happen if you are validating a challenge for a wildcard and a non-wildcard certificate at the same time. However, you should make sure to clean up old TXT records, because if the response size gets too big Let’s Encrypt will start rejecting it.
L38: 
L39: Pros:
L40:   * You can use this challenge to issue certificates containing wildcard domain names.
L41:   * It works well even if you have multiple web servers.
L42:   * You can use this challenge to validate domain names whose webservers aren’t exposed to the public internet.
L43: 
L44: Cons:
L45: 
L46:   * Keeping API credentials on your web server is risky.
L47:   * Your DNS provider might not offer an API.
L48:   * Your DNS API may not provide information on propagation times.
L49:   * It cannot be used to validate IP Addresses.
L50: # TLS-ALPN-01
L51: 
L52: This challenge was developed after TLS-SNI-01 became deprecated and is now standardized as cite34†RFC 8737†tools.ietf.org . Like TLS-SNI-01, it is performed via TLS on port 443. However, it uses a custom ALPN protocol to ensure that only servers that are aware of this challenge type will respond to validation requests. This also allows validation requests for this challenge type to use an SNI field that matches the domain name being validated, making it more secure.
L53: This challenge is not suitable for most people. It is best suited to authors of TLS-terminating reverse proxies that want to perform host-based validation like HTTP-01, but want to do it entirely at the TLS layer in order to separate concerns. Right now that mainly means large hosting providers.
L54: 
L55: Pros:
L56: 
L57:   * It works if port 80 is unavailable to you.
L58:   * It can be performed purely at the TLS layer.
L59:   * It can be used to validate IP Addresses as well.
L60: 
L61: Cons:
L62:   * ACME client support is limited.
L63:   * Like HTTP-01, if you have multiple servers they need to all answer with the same content.
L64:   * This method cannot be used to validate wildcard domains.
L65: # TLS-SNI-01
L66: 
L67: This challenge was defined in draft versions of ACME. It did a TLS handshake on port 443 and sent a specific cite35†SNI†en.wikipedia.org header, looking for a certificate that contained the token. It cite36†was removed in March 2019†community.letsencrypt.org because it was not secure enough.

L46: # Migrating WordPress
L47: ## In this article
L48: 
L49:   * cite28†Changing The Site URL L50:     * cite29†Moving Sites L51:   * cite30†Moving WordPress L52:     * cite31†Moving to a New Server L53:       * cite32†Keeping Your Domain Name and URLs L54:       * cite33†Changing Your Domain Name and URLs L55:     * cite34†Moving Directories On Your Existing Server L56:     * cite35†Managing Your Old Site L57:       * cite36†Shutting It Down L58:     * cite37†Moving WordPress Multisite L59:       * cite38†Related Links L60:     * cite39†Migrating multiple blogs into WordPress multisite L61:       * cite40†Steps to Follow L62: Copy page cite41†View as Markdown L63: 
L64: cite42†Back to top L65: ## cite28†Changing The Site URL L66: 
L67: On the `Settings -> General` screen in a single site installation of WordPress, there are two fields named “WordPress Address (URL)” and “Site Address (URL)”. They are important settings since they control where WordPress is located. These settings control the display of the URL in the admin section of your page, as well as the front end, and are used throughout the WordPress code.
L68:   * The “Site Address (URL)” setting is the address you want people to type in their browser to reach your WordPress blog.
L69:   * The “WordPress Address (URL)” setting is the address where your WordPress core files reside.
L70: 
L71: Note: Both settings should include the https:// part and should not have a slash `/` at the end.
L72: Every once in a while, somebody finds a need to manually change (or fix) these settings. Usually, this happens when they change one or both and discover that their site no longer works properly. This can leave the user with no easily discoverable way to correct the problem. This article tells you how to change these settings directly.
L73: Additional information is presented here for the case where you are moving WordPress from one site to another, as this will also require changing the site URL. You should not attempt to use this additional information if you’re only attempting to correct a “broken” site.
L74: 
L75: Alert! These directions are for single installs of WordPress only. If you are using WordPress MultiSite, you will need to manually edit your database.
L76: There are four easy methods to change the Site URL manually. Any of these methods will work and perform much the same function.
L77: #### cite43†Edit wp-config.php L78: 
L79: It is possible to set the site URL manually in the `wp-config.php` file.
L80: 
L81: Add these two lines to your `wp-config.php`, where “example.com” is the correct location of your site.
L82: 
L83:     `define( 'WP_HOME', 'https://example.com' );
L84:     define( 'WP_SITEURL', 'https://example.com' );
L85:     `
L86: 
L87: This is not necessarily the best fix, it’s just hard-coding the values into the site itself. You won’t be able to edit them on the General settings page anymore when using this method.
L88: #### cite44†Edit functions.php L89: 
L90: If you have access to the site via FTP, then this method will help you quickly get a site back up and running, if you changed those values incorrectly.
L91:   1. FTP to the site, and get a copy of the active theme’s functions.php file. You’re going to edit it in a simple text editor and upload it back to the site.
L92:   2. Add these two lines to the file, immediately after the initial `<?php` line:
L93: 
L94:     `update_option( 'siteurl', 'https://example.com' );
L95:     update_option( 'home', 'https://example.com' );
L96:     `
L97: 
L98: Obviously, use your own URL instead of `example.com`.
L99:   1. Upload the file back to your site, in the same location. FileZilla offers a handy “edit file” function to do all of the above rapidly; if you can use that, do so.
L100:   2. Load the login or admin page a couple of times. The site should come back up.
L101: 
L102: Important! Do not leave this code in the `functions.php` file. Remove them after the site is up and running again.
L103: Note: If your theme doesn’t have a `functions.php` file create a new one with a text editor. Add the `<?php` tag and the two lines using your own URL instead of `example.com`:
L104: 
L105:     `<?php
L106:     update_option( 'siteurl', 'https://example.com' );
L107:     update_option( 'home', 'https://example.com' );
L108:     `
L109: 
L110: Upload this file to your theme directory. Remove the lines or remove the file after the site is up and running again.
L111: #### cite45†LAN-based site to externally accessible site L112: 
L113: Here are some additional details that step you through transferring a LAN-based WordPress site into an externally accessible site, as well as enabling editing the wordpress site from inside the LAN.
L114: 
L115: Two important keys are router/firewall modifications and the “wait 10+ minutes” after making the changes at the end.
L116: 
L117:   1. Using SSH to log into your server (nano is a server preinstalled text editor):
L118: `$ nano /var/www/books/wp-content/themes/twentyeleven/functions.php`
L119: 
L120:   1. Add lines just after `<?php`
L121: 
L122:     `update_option( 'siteurl', 'https://example.com:port/yourblog');
L123:     update_option( 'home', 'https://example.com:port/yourblog');
L124:     `
L125: 
L126:   1. Refresh your web browser using your external site URL:
L127: 
L128: https://example.com:port/yourblog
L129: `$ nano /var/www/books/wp-content/themes/twentyeleven/functions.php`
L130: 
L131:   1. Remove those lines you just added (or comment them out)
L132:   2. Access your router, these steps are for pfSense, other routers should have similar settings to look for/watch out for)
L133: 
L134:   3. Add to firewall/nat table a line like this
L135: 
L136: `wan/tcp/port/LAN.server.IP/80`
L137: 
L138:   1. Add to firewall/rules table a line like this:
L139: 
L140: `tcp/*/port/LAN.server.IP/port/*`
L141: 
L142:   1. Uncheck the box at System/advanced/network address translation/Disable NAT Reflection
L143: `"Disables the automatic creation of NAT redirect rules for access to your public IP addresses from within your internal networks. Note: Reflection only works on port forward type items and does not work for large ranges > 500 ports."`
L144: 
L145:   1. Then go do something for ten minutes and when you get back see if the external url https://example.com:port/yourblog from a LAN browser brings the page up correctly.
L146: #### cite46†Relocate method L147: 
L148: WordPress supports an automatic relocation method intended to be a quick assist to getting a site working when relocating a site from one server to another.
L149: #### cite47†Code function L150: When RELOCATE has been defined as true in `wp-config.php` (see next chapter), the following code in `wp-login.php` will take action:
L151: 
L152:     `if ( defined( 'RELOCATE' ) AND RELOCATE ) {
L153:         // Move flag is set
L154:         if ( isset( $_SERVER['PATH_INFO'] ) AND ($_SERVER['PATH_INFO'] != $_SERVER['PHP_SELF']) )
L155:             $_SERVER['PHP_SELF'] = str_replace( $_SERVER['PATH_INFO'], "", $_SERVER['PHP_SELF'] );
L156:         $url = dirname( set_url_scheme( 'https://'. $_SERVER['HTTP_HOST'] . $_SERVER['PHP_SELF'] ) );
L157:         if ( $url != get_option( 'siteurl' ) )
L158:             update_option( 'siteurl', $url );
L159:     }
L160:     `
L161: Steps
L162:   1. Edit the `wp-config.php` file.
L163:   2. After the “define” statements (just before the comment line that says “That’s all, stop editing!”), insert a new line, and type: `define('RELOCATE',true);`
L164:   3. Save your `wp-config.php` file.
"}

require "yaml"

module HetznerDeployConfig
  CONFIG_PATH = File.expand_path("../../config/deploy.hetzner.shared.yml", __dir__)
  MissingConfigError = Class.new(StandardError)

  class << self
    def app_host
      fetch("app_host")
    end

    def app_host_if_present
      fetch("app_host", required: false)
    end

    def web_host
      fetch("web_host")
    end

    def ssh_host_key
      fetch("ssh_host_key")
    end

    def fetch(key, required: true)
      loaded_config = config(required:)
      return unless loaded_config

      loaded_config.fetch(key)
    end

    private

    def config(required: true)
      return @config if instance_variable_defined?(:@config)

      unless File.exist?(config_path)
        if required
          raise MissingConfigError, "Missing Hetzner deploy config at #{config_path}"
        end

        @config = nil
        return
      end

      @config = YAML.safe_load_file(config_path) || {}
    end

    def config_path
      CONFIG_PATH
    end
  end
end

L133: 
L134:     `  forward_headers: true
L135:     `
L136: ## cite35†Response timeout L137: 
L138: How long to wait for requests to complete before timing out, defaults to 30 seconds:
L139: 
L140:     `  response_timeout: 10
L141:     `
L142: ## cite36†Path-based routing L143: 
L144: For applications that split their traffic to different services based on the request path, you can use path-based routing to mount services under different path prefixes. Usage sample: path_prefix: ‘/api’
L145: 
L146: You can also specify multiple paths in two ways.
L147: 
L148: When using path_prefix you can supply multiple routes separated by commas.
L149: 
L150:     `  path_prefix: "/api,/oauth_callback"
L151:     `
L152: You can also specify paths as a list of paths, the configuration will be rolled together into a comma separated string.
L153: 
L154:     `  path_prefixes:
L155:         - "/api"
L156:         - "/oauth_callback"
L157:     `
L158: 
L159: By default, the path prefix will be stripped from the request before it is forwarded upstream.
L160: 
L161: So in the example above, a request to /api/users/123 will be forwarded to web-1 as /users/123.
L162: To instead forward the request with the original path (including the prefix), specify –strip-path-prefix=false
L163: 
L164:     `  strip_path_prefix: false
L165:     `
L166: ## cite37†Healthcheck L167: 
L168: When deploying, the proxy will by default hit `/up` once every second until we hit the deploy timeout, with a 5-second timeout for each request.
L169: 
L170: Once the app is up, the proxy will stop hitting the healthcheck endpoint.
L171: 
L172:     `  healthcheck:
L173:         interval: 3
L174:         path: /health
L175:         timeout: 3
L176:     `
L177: ## cite38†Buffering L178: 
L179: Whether to buffer request and response bodies in the proxy.
L180: 
L181: By default, buffering is enabled with a max request body size of 1GB and no limit for response size.
L182: 
L183: You can also set the memory limit for buffering, which defaults to 1MB; anything larger than that is written to disk.

L186:         requests: true
L187:         responses: true
L188:         max_request_body: 40_000_000
L189:         max_response_body: 0
L190:         memory: 2_000_000
L191:     `
L192: ## cite39†Logging L193: 
L194: Configure request logging for the proxy. You can specify request and response headers to log. By default, `Cache-Control`, `Last-Modified`, and `User-Agent` request headers are logged:

L199:           - X-Forwarded-Proto
L200:         response_headers:
L201:           - X-Request-ID
L202:           - X-Request-Start
L203:     `

Die vorhandene Infrastruktur eignet sich grundsätzlich dafür: Beide Apps laufen bereits auf demselben Hetzner-Server. Für Staging scheinen aktuell ausreichende Reserven vorhanden; die Ressourcen müssen trotzdem begrenzt werden.

Der Ablauf zeichnet sich so ab:

1. **Bestand sichern:** DNS-Einstellungen, bisherige Websites, Datenbanken, Medien und Deployment-Konfigurationen sichern; Rückweg festlegen.
2. **Alte Websites vorbereiten:** `old.stuttgart-live.de` und `old.russ-live.de` inklusive HTTPS einrichten und vor dem Hauptdomainwechsel prüfen. Bei WordPress müssen auch interne URLs und Weiterleitungen angepasst werden.
3. **Staging aufbauen:** Je Projekt eigene Container, Datenbanken, Zugangsdaten und Medienkopien. Russ-Staging liest ausschließlich aus Stuttgart-Staging. Gleiche Software und Deployment-Technik wie Produktion, mit weniger Prozessen.
4. **Staging absichern und testen:** Passwortschutz, Suchmaschinen ausschließen, E-Mails abfangen und echte Newsletter-/Social-Media-Veröffentlichungen verhindern.
5. **Produktionsumzug vorbereiten:** HTTPS, `www`-Weiterleitungen, alte URL-Pfade, Newsletter-Links und externe Integrationen prüfen. Bestehende Microsoft-365-Mail-Einträge erhalten; bisherige IPv6-Webeinträge berücksichtigen.
6. **Nacheinander umschalten:** Zunächst Russ Live, anschließend Stuttgart Live; jeweils mit Abnahme und Rückfallmöglichkeit.
7. **Nachkontrolle und Dokumentation:** Erreichbarkeit, Bilder, Anmeldung, Mail, Fehler und Zertifikate prüfen; Betriebsanleitung aktualisieren.

**Hast du neben der Domainverwaltung auch Zugriff auf das bisherige WordPress-Hosting und die WordPress-Administration?** Der Domainzugang allein reicht für diese Anpassungen nicht aus.

Nein, ich habe keinen Zugriff auf das bisherige WordPress-Hosting. Wozu benötige ich das?

Den Hostingzugriff benötigen wir für **die bisherige WordPress-Seite unter `old.stuttgart-live.de`**. Dafür sind drei Anpassungen nötig:

- **DNS:** `old.stuttgart-live.de` auf den bisherigen Webserver zeigen lassen. Das geht über deine Domainverwaltung.
- **Hosting:** Dem Webserver die zusätzliche Adresse zuordnen und ein gültiges HTTPS-Zertifikat einrichten.
- **WordPress:** Die Website-Adresse und gegebenenfalls gespeicherte Links auf `old.stuttgart-live.de` anpassen. [WordPress-Dokumentation](https://developer.wordpress.org/advanced-administration/upgrade/migrating/)

**Nur der DNS-Eintrag genügt nicht zuverlässig:** Die alte Seite könnte sonst auf `stuttgart-live.de` zurückleiten oder Bilder und Links von dort laden – nach dem Umzug wäre das bereits die neue Rails-Anwendung.

Du brauchst den Zugang nicht selbst. Der bisherige Betreiber kann diese Anpassungen übernehmen. Der Umzug der beiden Rails-Apps und der Aufbau von Staging können unabhängig davon vorbereitet werden.

L46: # Migrating WordPress
L47: ## In this article
L48: 
L49:   * cite28†Changing The Site URL L50:     * cite29†Moving Sites L51:   * cite30†Moving WordPress L52:     * cite31†Moving to a New Server L53:       * cite32†Keeping Your Domain Name and URLs L54:       * cite33†Changing Your Domain Name and URLs L55:     * cite34†Moving Directories On Your Existing Server L56:     * cite35†Managing Your Old Site L57:       * cite36†Shutting It Down L58:     * cite37†Moving WordPress Multisite L59:       * cite38†Related Links L60:     * cite39†Migrating multiple blogs into WordPress multisite L61:       * cite40†Steps to Follow L62: Copy page cite41†View as Markdown L63: 
L64: cite42†Back to top L65: ## cite28†Changing The Site URL L66: 
L67: On the `Settings -> General` screen in a single site installation of WordPress, there are two fields named “WordPress Address (URL)” and “Site Address (URL)”. They are important settings since they control where WordPress is located. These settings control the display of the URL in the admin section of your page, as well as the front end, and are used throughout the WordPress code.
L68:   * The “Site Address (URL)” setting is the address you want people to type in their browser to reach your WordPress blog.
L69:   * The “WordPress Address (URL)” setting is the address where your WordPress core files reside.
L70: 
L71: Note: Both settings should include the https:// part and should not have a slash `/` at the end.
L72: Every once in a while, somebody finds a need to manually change (or fix) these settings. Usually, this happens when they change one or both and discover that their site no longer works properly. This can leave the user with no easily discoverable way to correct the problem. This article tells you how to change these settings directly.
L73: Additional information is presented here for the case where you are moving WordPress from one site to another, as this will also require changing the site URL. You should not attempt to use this additional information if you’re only attempting to correct a “broken” site.
L74: 
L75: Alert! These directions are for single installs of WordPress only. If you are using WordPress MultiSite, you will need to manually edit your database.
L76: There are four easy methods to change the Site URL manually. Any of these methods will work and perform much the same function.
L77: #### cite43†Edit wp-config.php L78: 
L79: It is possible to set the site URL manually in the `wp-config.php` file.
L80: 
L81: Add these two lines to your `wp-config.php`, where “example.com” is the correct location of your site.
L82: 
L83:     `define( 'WP_HOME', 'https://example.com' );
L84:     define( 'WP_SITEURL', 'https://example.com' );
L85:     `
L86: 
L87: This is not necessarily the best fix, it’s just hard-coding the values into the site itself. You won’t be able to edit them on the General settings page anymore when using this method.
L88: #### cite44†Edit functions.php L89: 
L90: If you have access to the site via FTP, then this method will help you quickly get a site back up and running, if you changed those values incorrectly.
L91:   1. FTP to the site, and get a copy of the active theme’s functions.php file. You’re going to edit it in a simple text editor and upload it back to the site.
L92:   2. Add these two lines to the file, immediately after the initial `<?php` line:
L93: 
L94:     `update_option( 'siteurl', 'https://example.com' );
L95:     update_option( 'home', 'https://example.com' );
L96:     `
L97: 
L98: Obviously, use your own URL instead of `example.com`.
L99:   1. Upload the file back to your site, in the same location. FileZilla offers a handy “edit file” function to do all of the above rapidly; if you can use that, do so.
L100:   2. Load the login or admin page a couple of times. The site should come back up.
L101: 
L102: Important! Do not leave this code in the `functions.php` file. Remove them after the site is up and running again.
L103: Note: If your theme doesn’t have a `functions.php` file create a new one with a text editor. Add the `<?php` tag and the two lines using your own URL instead of `example.com`:
L104: 
L105:     `<?php
L106:     update_option( 'siteurl', 'https://example.com' );
L107:     update_option( 'home', 'https://example.com' );
L108:     `
L109: 
L110: Upload this file to your theme directory. Remove the lines or remove the file after the site is up and running again.
L111: #### cite45†LAN-based site to externally accessible site L112: 
L113: Here are some additional details that step you through transferring a LAN-based WordPress site into an externally accessible site, as well as enabling editing the wordpress site from inside the LAN.
L114: 
L115: Two important keys are router/firewall modifications and the “wait 10+ minutes” after making the changes at the end.
L116: 
L117:   1. Using SSH to log into your server (nano is a server preinstalled text editor):
L118: `$ nano /var/www/books/wp-content/themes/twentyeleven/functions.php`
L119: 
L120:   1. Add lines just after `<?php`
L121: 
L122:     `update_option( 'siteurl', 'https://example.com:port/yourblog');
L123:     update_option( 'home', 'https://example.com:port/yourblog');
L124:     `
L125: 
L126:   1. Refresh your web browser using your external site URL:
L127: 
L128: https://example.com:port/yourblog
L129: `$ nano /var/www/books/wp-content/themes/twentyeleven/functions.php`
L130: 
L131:   1. Remove those lines you just added (or comment them out)
L132:   2. Access your router, these steps are for pfSense, other routers should have similar settings to look for/watch out for)
L133: 
L134:   3. Add to firewall/nat table a line like this
L135: 
L136: `wan/tcp/port/LAN.server.IP/80`
L137: 
L138:   1. Add to firewall/rules table a line like this:
L139: 
L140: `tcp/*/port/LAN.server.IP/port/*`
L141: 
L142:   1. Uncheck the box at System/advanced/network address translation/Disable NAT Reflection
L143: `"Disables the automatic creation of NAT redirect rules for access to your public IP addresses from within your internal networks. Note: Reflection only works on port forward type items and does not work for large ranges > 500 ports."`
L144: 
L145:   1. Then go do something for ten minutes and when you get back see if the external url https://example.com:port/yourblog from a LAN browser brings the page up correctly.
L146: #### cite46†Relocate method L147: 
L148: WordPress supports an automatic relocation method intended to be a quick assist to getting a site working when relocating a site from one server to another.
L149: #### cite47†Code function L150: When RELOCATE has been defined as true in `wp-config.php` (see next chapter), the following code in `wp-login.php` will take action:
L151: 
L152:     `if ( defined( 'RELOCATE' ) AND RELOCATE ) {
L153:         // Move flag is set
L154:         if ( isset( $_SERVER['PATH_INFO'] ) AND ($_SERVER['PATH_INFO'] != $_SERVER['PHP_SELF']) )
L155:             $_SERVER['PHP_SELF'] = str_replace( $_SERVER['PATH_INFO'], "", $_SERVER['PHP_SELF'] );
L156:         $url = dirname( set_url_scheme( 'https://'. $_SERVER['HTTP_HOST'] . $_SERVER['PHP_SELF'] ) );
L157:         if ( $url != get_option( 'siteurl' ) )
L158:             update_option( 'siteurl', $url );
L159:     }
L160:     `
L161: Steps
L162:   1. Edit the `wp-config.php` file.
L163:   2. After the “define” statements (just before the comment line that says “That’s all, stop editing!”), insert a new line, and type: `define('RELOCATE',true);`
L164:   3. Save your `wp-config.php` file.
L165:   4. Open a web browser and manually point it to `wp-login.php` on the new server. For example, if your new site is at https://www.example.com, then type https://www.example.com/wp-login.php into your browser’s address bar.
L166:   5. Login as per normal.
L167:   6. Look in your web browser’s address bar to verify that you have, indeed, logged in to the correct server. If this is the case, then in the Admin back-end, navigate to `Settings > General` and verify that both the address settings are correct. Remember to Save Changes.
L168:   7. Once this has been fixed, edit `wp-config.php` and either completely remove the line that you added (delete the whole line), comment it out (with `//`) or change the true value to false if you think it’s likely you will be relocating again.
L169: Note: When the `RELOCATE` flag is set to true, the Site URL will be automatically updated to whatever path you are using to access the login screen. This will get the admin section up and running on the new URL, but it will not correct any other part of the setup. You’ll still need to alter those manually.
L170: Important! Leaving the RELOCATE constant in your `wp-config.php` file is insecure, as it allows an attacker to change your site URL to anything they want in some configurations. Always remove the RELOCATE line from `wp-config.php` after you’re done.
L171: #### cite48†Changing the URL directly in the database L172: 
L173: If you know how to access phpMyAdmin on your host, then you can edit these values directly to get your site up and running again.
L174:   1. cite49†Backup your database and save the copy off-site.
L175:   2. Login to cite50†phpMyAdmin .
L176:   3. Click the link to your Databases.
L177:   4. A list of your databases will appear. Choose the one that is your WordPress database.
L178:   5. All the tables in your database will appear on the screen.
L179:   6. From the list, look for `wp_options`. Note: The table prefix of `wp_` may be different if you changed it when installing.
L180:   7. Click on the small icon indicated as Browse.
L181:   8. A screen will open with a list of the fields within the wp_options table.
L182:   9. Under the field option_name, scroll down and look for `siteurl`.
L183:   10. Click the Edit Field icon which usually is found at the far left at the beginning of the row.
L184:   11. The Edit Field window will appear.
L185:   12. In the input box for option_value, carefully change the URL information to the new address.
L186:   13. Verify this is correct and click Go to save the information.
L187:   14. You should be returned to your `wp_options` table.
L188:   15. Look for the home field in the table and click Edit Field. Note: There are several pages of tables inside `wp_options`. Look for the > symbol to page through them.
L189:   16. In the input box for option_value, carefully change the URL information to the new address.
L190:   17. Verify this is correct and click Go to save the information.
L191: ### cite29†Moving Sites L192: 
L193: When moving sites from one location to another, it is sometimes necessary to manually modify data in the database to make the new site URL information to be recognized properly. Many tools exist to assist with this, and those should generally be used instead of manual modifications.
L194: 
L195: This is presented here as information only. This data may not be complete or accurate.
L196: You should read the cite51†Moving WordPress article first, if attempting to move WordPress from one system to another.
L197: #### cite52†Altering Table Prefixes L198: 
L199: Like many WordPress administrators, you may be running several WordPress installations off of one database using various `wp-config.php` hacks. Many of these hacks involve dynamically setting table prefixes, and if you do end up altering your table prefix, you must update several entries within the `prefix_usermeta` table as well.
L200: 
L201: As in the above section, remember that SQL changes are permanent and so you should back up your database first:
L202: If you are changing table prefixes for a site, then remember to alter the table prefix in the usermeta tables as well. This will allow the new site to properly recognize user permissions from the old site.
L203: 
L204:     `UPDATE `newprefix_usermeta` SET `meta_key` = REPLACE( `meta_key` , 'oldprefix_', 'newprefix_' );
L205:     `
L206: #### cite53†Changing Template Files L207: In your WordPress Theme, open each template file and search for any manually entered references to your old domain name and replace it with the new one. Look for specific hand-coded links you may have entered on the various template files such as the `sidebar.php` and `footer.php`. WordPress uses a template tag called `bloginfo()` to automatically generate your site address from information entered in your Administration > Settings > General panel.
L208: The tag in your template files will not have to be modified.
L209: #### cite54†Changing the Config file L210: 
L211: You will need to update your WordPress configuration file if your database has moved or changed in certain ways.
L212:   1. You will only need to modify the config file if:
L213:      * your database has moved to another server and is not running on your localhost
L214:      * you have renamed your database
L215:      * you have changed the database user name
L216:   2. Make a backup copy of your `wp-config.php` file.
L217:   3. Open the `wp-config.php` file in a cite55†text editor†wordpress.org .
L218:   4. Review its contents. In particular, you are looking for the cite56†database host entry .
L219:   5. Save the file.

**Direkt über die IP funktioniert es aktuell nicht.** Ich habe den bisherigen Server geprüft:

- `http://83.169.28.13` antwortet mit **403 Forbidden**.
- `https://83.169.28.13` verursacht einen **Zertifikatsfehler**.
- Mit dem ursprünglichen Domainnamen `stuttgart-live.de` liefert derselbe Server die Seite aus.

Der Server benötigt also den Domainnamen, um die richtige Website auszuwählen. WordPress verwendet diese Adresse außerdem für seine internen Links. [WordPress-Dokumentation](https://developer.wordpress.org/advanced-administration/upgrade/migrating/)

**Für einen gelegentlichen internen Zugriff gibt es eine einfache Möglichkeit:** Auf ausgewählten Rechnern lässt sich über die lokale `hosts`-Datei festlegen, dass `stuttgart-live.de` weiterhin den alten Server öffnet. Alle anderen Besucher erreichen nach dem Umzug die neue Seite. Zum Testen der neuen Produktion müsste diese lokale Einstellung wieder entfernt werden. Das funktioniert nur, solange das bisherige Hosting weiterläuft; auch das bisherige HTTPS-Zertifikat wird irgendwann ablaufen.

Für ein öffentlich erreichbares Archiv unter `old.stuttgart-live.de` wäre alternativ eine **statische Kopie der öffentlich sichtbaren Seiten** möglich. Diese müsste vor dem Umzug erstellt und auf Vollständigkeit geprüft werden; WordPress-Funktionen wären darin nicht enthalten.

**Reicht euch der interne Zugriff zum Nachschlagen, oder soll die bisherige Seite weiterhin öffentlich erreichbar bleiben?**

#!/bin/bash -e

# If running the Rails server then create or migrate existing databases.
if { [ "${@: -2:1}" == "./bin/rails" ] && [ "${@: -1:1}" == "server" ]; } || [ "${1:-}" == "./bin/production-server" ]; then
  ./bin/rails db:prepare
fi

exec "${@}"
require "active_support/core_ext/integer/time"
require Rails.root.join("app/lib/hetzner_deploy_config").to_s

Rails.application.configure do
  # The Docker image build excludes deploy config files. Kamal injects APP_HOST
  # at runtime from the shared Hetzner deploy config.
  app_host = ENV["APP_HOST"].presence || HetznerDeployConfig.app_host_if_present

  # Settings specified here will take precedence over those in config/application.rb.

  # Code is not reloaded between requests.
  config.enable_reloading = false

  # Eager load code on boot for better performance and memory savings (ignored by Rake tasks).
  config.eager_load = true

  # Full error reports are disabled.
  config.consider_all_requests_local = false

  # Turn on fragment caching in view templates.
  config.action_controller.perform_caching = true

  # Cache assets for far-future expiry since they are all digest stamped.
  config.public_file_server.headers = { "cache-control" => "public, max-age=#{1.year.to_i}" }

  # Enable serving of images, stylesheets, and JavaScripts from an asset server.
  # config.asset_host = "http://assets.example.com"

  # Use the shared local disk volume on Hetzner by default, but allow overriding.
  config.active_storage.service = ENV.fetch("ACTIVE_STORAGE_SERVICE", "local").to_sym

  # Assume all access to the app is happening through a SSL-terminating reverse proxy.
  config.assume_ssl = true

  # Force all access to the app over SSL, use Strict-Transport-Security, and use secure cookies.
  config.force_ssl = true

  # Skip http-to-https redirect for the default health check endpoint.
  # config.ssl_options = { redirect: { exclude: ->(request) { request.path == "/up" } } }

  # Log to STDOUT with the current request id as a default log tag.
  config.log_tags = [ :request_id ]
  config.logger   = ActiveSupport::TaggedLogging.logger(STDOUT)

  # Change to "debug" to log everything (including potentially personally-identifiable information!).
  config.log_level = ENV.fetch("RAILS_LOG_LEVEL", "info")

  # Prevent health checks from clogging up the logs.
  config.silence_healthcheck_path = "/up"

  # Don't log any deprecations.
  config.active_support.report_deprecations = false

  # Replace the default in-process memory cache store with a durable alternative.
  config.cache_store = :solid_cache_store

  # Replace the default in-process and non-durable queuing backend for Active Job.
  config.active_job.queue_adapter = :solid_queue
  config.solid_queue.connects_to = { database: { writing: :queue } }

  # Ignore bad email addresses and do not raise email delivery errors.
  # Set this to true and configure the email server for immediate delivery to raise delivery errors.
  # config.action_mailer.raise_delivery_errors = false

  # Set host to be used by links generated in mailer templates.
  config.action_mailer.default_url_options = { host: app_host, protocol: "https" }.compact

  # Specify outgoing SMTP server. Remember to add smtp/* credentials via bin/rails credentials:edit.
  # config.action_mailer.smtp_settings = {
  #   user_name: Rails.application.credentials.dig(:smtp, :user_name),
  #   password: Rails.application.credentials.dig(:smtp, :password),
  #   address: "smtp.example.com",
  #   port: 587,
  #   authentication: :plain
  # }

  # Enable locale fallbacks for I18n (makes lookups for any locale fall back to
  # the I18n.default_locale when a translation cannot be found).
  config.i18n.fallbacks = true

  # Do not dump schema after migrations.
  config.active_record.dump_schema_after_migration = false

  # Only use :id for inspections in production.
  config.active_record.attributes_for_inspect = [ :id ]

  # Enable DNS rebinding protection and other `Host` header attacks.
  # config.hosts = [
  #   "example.com",     # Allow requests from example.com
  #   /.*\.example\.com/ # Allow requests from subdomains like `www.example.com`
  # ]
  #
  # Skip DNS rebinding protection for the default health check endpoint.
  # config.host_authorization = { exclude: ->(request) { request.path == "/up" } }
end

name: CI

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  scan_ruby:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Set up Ruby
        uses: ruby/setup-ruby@v1
        with:
          bundler-cache: true

      - name: Scan for common Rails security vulnerabilities using static analysis
        run: bin/brakeman --no-pager
      
      - name: Scan for known security vulnerabilities in gems used
        run: bin/bundler-audit
      
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    env:
      RUBOCOP_CACHE_ROOT: tmp/rubocop
    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Set up Ruby
        uses: ruby/setup-ruby@v1
        with:
          bundler-cache: true

      - name: Prepare RuboCop cache
        uses: actions/cache@v6
        env:
          DEPENDENCIES_HASH: ${{ hashFiles('.ruby-version', '**/.rubocop.yml', '**/.rubocop_todo.yml', 'Gemfile.lock') }}
        with:
          path: ${{ env.RUBOCOP_CACHE_ROOT }}
          key: rubocop-${{ runner.os }}-${{ env.DEPENDENCIES_HASH }}-${{ github.ref_name == github.event.repository.default_branch && github.run_id || 'default' }}
          restore-keys: |
            rubocop-${{ runner.os }}-${{ env.DEPENDENCIES_HASH }}-

      - name: Lint code for consistent style
        run: bin/rubocop -f github

  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres
        env:
          POSTGRES_USER: postgres
          POSTGRES_PASSWORD: postgres
        ports:
          - 5432:5432
        options: --health-cmd="pg_isready" --health-interval=10s --health-timeout=5s --health-retries=3

      # redis:
      #   image: valkey/valkey:8
      #   ports:
      #     - 6379:6379
      #   options: --health-cmd "redis-cli ping" --health-interval 10s --health-timeout 5s --health-retries 5

    steps:
      - name: Install packages
        run: sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install --no-install-recommends -y libpq-dev libvips node-gyp

      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v7

      - name: Set up Ruby
        uses: ruby/setup-ruby@v1
        with:
          bundler-cache: true

      - name: Run tests
        env:
          RAILS_ENV: test
          DB_HOST: localhost
          DB_PORT: 5432
          DB_USER: postgres
          DB_PASSWORD: postgres

# This Dockerfile is designed for production, not development. Use with Kamal or build'n'run by hand:

# Make sure RUBY_VERSION matches the Ruby version in .ruby-version
ARG RUBY_VERSION=4.0.2
FROM docker.io/library/ruby:$RUBY_VERSION-slim AS base

# Rails app lives here
WORKDIR /rails

# Install base packages
RUN apt-get update -qq && \
    apt-get install --no-install-recommends -y curl ffmpeg fontconfig gettext-base libjemalloc2 libvips nginx postgresql-client && \
    ln -s /usr/lib/$(uname -m)-linux-gnu/libjemalloc.so.2 /usr/local/lib/libjemalloc.so && \
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists /var/cache/apt/archives

# Set production environment variables and enable jemalloc for reduced memory usage and latency.
ENV RAILS_ENV="production" \
    BUNDLE_DEPLOYMENT="1" \
    BUNDLE_PATH="/usr/local/bundle" \
    BUNDLE_WITHOUT="development" \
    LD_PRELOAD="/usr/local/lib/libjemalloc.so"

# Throw-away build stage to reduce size of final image
FROM base AS build

# Install packages needed to build gems and node modules
RUN apt-get update -qq && \
    apt-get install --no-install-recommends -y build-essential git libpq-dev libyaml-dev node-gyp pkg-config python-is-python3 && \
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists /var/cache/apt/archives

# Install JavaScript dependencies
ARG NODE_VERSION=24.11.1
ARG YARN_VERSION=latest
ENV PATH=/usr/local/node/bin:$PATH
RUN curl -sL https://github.com/nodenv/node-build/archive/master.tar.gz | tar xz -C /tmp/ && \
    /tmp/node-build-master/bin/node-build "${NODE_VERSION}" /usr/local/node && \
    rm -rf /tmp/node-build-master
RUN corepack enable && yarn set version $YARN_VERSION

# Install application gems
COPY vendor/* ./vendor/
COPY Gemfile Gemfile.lock ./

RUN bundle install && \
    rm -rf ~/.bundle/ "${BUNDLE_PATH}"/ruby/*/cache "${BUNDLE_PATH}"/ruby/*/bundler/gems/*/.git && \
    # -j 1 disable parallel compilation to avoid a QEMU bug: https://github.com/rails/bootsnap/issues/495
    bundle exec bootsnap precompile -j 1 --gemfile

# Install node modules. The project uses bun.lock in development, so
# we install from package.json during image builds.
COPY package.json ./
RUN yarn install

# Copy application code
COPY . .

# Precompile bootsnap code for faster boot times.
# -j 1 disable parallel compilation to avoid a QEMU bug: https://github.com/rails/bootsnap/issues/495
RUN bundle exec bootsnap precompile -j 1 app/ lib/

# Precompiling assets for production without requiring secret RAILS_MASTER_KEY
RUN SECRET_KEY_BASE_DUMMY=1 ./bin/rails assets:precompile


RUN rm -rf node_modules


# Final stage for app image
FROM base

COPY vendor/fonts/runtime /usr/local/share/fonts/stuttgart-live
RUN fc-cache -f && \
    fc-match "Oswald" && \
    fc-match "Archivo Narrow"

# Run and own only the runtime files as a non-root user for security
RUN groupadd --system --gid 1000 rails && \
    useradd rails --uid 1000 --gid 1000 --create-home --shell /bin/bash
USER 1000:1000

# Copy built artifacts: gems, application
COPY --chown=rails:rails --from=build "${BUNDLE_PATH}" "${BUNDLE_PATH}"
COPY --chown=rails:rails --from=build /rails /rails

# Entrypoint prepares the database.
ENTRYPOINT ["/rails/bin/docker-entrypoint"]

# Start server via nginx + Puma by default, this can be overwritten at runtime
EXPOSE 80
CMD ["./bin/production-server"]

L53: You should be familiar with the syntax for GitHub Actions. For more information, see cite18†Writing workflows .
L54: ## cite6†Triggering your deployment L55: 
L56: You can use a variety of events to trigger your deployment workflow. Some of the most common are: `pull_request`, `push`, and `workflow_dispatch`.
L57: 
L58: For example, a workflow with the following triggers runs whenever:
L59:   * There is a push to the `main` branch.
L60:   * A pull request targeting the `main` branch is opened, synchronized, or reopened.
L61:   * Someone manually triggers it.
L62: 
L63:     `on:
L64:       push:
L65:         branches:
L66:           - main
L67:       pull_request:
L68:         branches:
L69:           - main
L70:       workflow_dispatch:
L71:     `
L72: 
L73: For more information, see cite19†Events that trigger workflows .
L74: ## cite7†Using environments L75: Environments are used to describe a general deployment target like `production`, `staging`, or `development`. When a GitHub Actions workflow deploys to an environment, the environment is displayed on the main page of the repository. You can use environments to require approval for a job to proceed, restrict which branches can trigger a workflow, gate deployments with custom deployment protection rules, or limit access to secrets.
L76: For more information about creating environments, see cite20†Managing environments for deployment .
L77: You can configure environments with protection rules and secrets. When a workflow job references an environment, the job won't start until all of the environment's protection rules pass. A job also cannot access secrets that are defined in an environment until all the deployment protection rules pass. To learn more, see cite13†Using custom deployment protection rules in this article.
L78: ## cite8†Using concurrency L79: 
L80: Concurrency ensures that only a single job or workflow using the same concurrency group will run at a time. You can use concurrency so that an environment has a maximum of one deployment in progress at a time. For more information about concurrency, see cite21†Control the concurrency of workflows and jobs .
L81: ## cite9†Using environments without deployments L82: By default, when a workflow job references an environment, GitHub creates a deployment object to track the deployment. You can opt out of deployment creation by setting `deployment` to `false` in the environment configuration. The valid values are `true` (default) and `false`. You can also use an expression, for example `deployment: ${{ github.ref_name == 'main' }}`.
L83: 
L84:     `jobs:
L85:       test:
L86:         runs-on: ubuntu-latest
L87:         environment:
L88:           name: staging
L89:           deployment: false
L90:         steps:
L91:           - name: run tests
L92:             env:
L93:               API_KEY: ${{ secrets.API_KEY }}
L94:             run: echo "Running tests with staging secrets"
L95:     `
L96: When `deployment` is set to `false`:
L97: 
L98:   * The job has full access to environment secrets and variables.
L99:   * No GitHub deployment object is created—the deployment history for the environment is not updated.
L100:   * Wait timer protection rules still apply—the job waits for the configured duration.
L101:   * Required reviewers still apply—reviewers must still approve before the job runs.
L102: 
L103: This is useful when you want to use environments for:
L104:   * Organizing secrets—group related secrets under an environment name without creating deployment records.
L105:   * Access control—restrict which branches can use certain secrets via environment branch policies, without deployment tracking.
L106:   * CI and testing jobs—reference an environment for its configuration without adding noise to the deployment history.
L107: ### cite22†Interaction with protection rules L108: 
L109: The `deployment` property controls which protection rules apply:
L110: 
L111: Protection rule  | `deployment: true` (default)  | `deployment: false`
L112: --- | --- | ---
L113: None  | Deployment created, job runs  | No deployment, job runs
L114: Wait timer  | Wait timer enforced  | Wait timer still enforced
L115: Required reviewers  | Reviewers must approve  | Reviewers must approve
L116: Custom deployment protection rule app  | App webhook sent, must approve  | Job fails with error
L117: Custom deployment protection rules (GitHub Apps) require a deployment object to function. If you set `deployment: false` on an environment that has custom deployment protection rules, the job will fail immediately with an annotation or error message explaining that the environment's protection rules are incompatible with `deployment: false`. Either remove `deployment: false` from your workflow, or remove the custom deployment protection rules from the environment.
L118: Note that `concurrency` and `environment` are not connected. The concurrency value can be any string; it does not need to be an environment name. Additionally, if another workflow uses the same environment but does not specify concurrency, that workflow will not be subject to any concurrency rules.
L119: For example, when the following workflow runs, it will be paused with the status `pending` if any job or workflow that uses the `production` concurrency group is in progress. It will also cancel any job or workflow that uses the `production` concurrency group and has the status `pending`. This means that there will be a maximum of one running and one pending job or workflow in that uses the `production` concurrency group.

L121:     `name: Deployment
L122: 
L123:     concurrency: production
L124: 
L125:     on:
L126:       push:
L127:         branches:
L128:           - main
L129: 
L130:     jobs:
L131:       deployment:
L132:         runs-on: ubuntu-latest
L133:         environment: production
L134:         steps:
L135:           - name: deploy
L136:             # ...deployment-specific steps
L137:     `
L138: You can also specify concurrency at the job level. This will allow other jobs in the workflow to proceed even if the concurrent job is `pending`.

L142:     on:
L143:       push:
L144:         branches:
L145:           - main
L146: 
L147:     jobs:
L148:       deployment:
L149:         runs-on: ubuntu-latest
L150:         environment: production
L151:         concurrency: production
L152:         steps:
L153:           - name: deploy
L154:             # ...deployment-specific steps
L155:     `
L156: You can also use `cancel-in-progress` to cancel any currently running job or workflow in the same concurrency group.
